citation: 'Bird’s-Eye View of Old Fort Dearborn.' Illustration at p. 27 of J. Seymour Currey, The Story of Old Fort Dearborn (Chicago: A. C. McClurg & Co., 1912). Numbered reconstruction of the first fort, not a contemporary view.
author: Illustrator uncredited in the consulted caption; J. Seymour Currey is the book author
describes_date: the first Fort Dearborn, 1803–1812, reconstructed retrospectively
repository: Wikimedia Commons, File:Birds_eye_view_of_first_Fort_Dearborn.jpg; also reproduced in Project Gutenberg eBook 52346, images/old_fort_dearborn.png
locator: Printed page 27, numbered bird’s-eye reconstruction; caption and list of illustrations in the inspected Gutenberg edition.
rights_note: Published in the United States in 1912, now out of copyright there; Commons explicitly marks this picture Public domain due to date of publication (1912).
access_notes: Inspected the actual local 889 x 588 image and consulted the Commons description plus Gutenberg illustrated HTML on 2026-10-23. The Gutenberg list of illustrations and caption confirm The Story of Old Fort Dearborn, p. 27; the local IMAGE_SOURCES.md instead names Chicago: Its History and Its Builders, which is not followed here. Commons says the picture follows a drawing of Albert L. Van den Berghen’s 1898 model published by the Chicago Daily Tribune on 5 March 1899; that newspaper and model were not independently inspected.
what_it_supplies: Two-storey courtyard gallery treatment on the visible inner barracks/quarters ranges: an upper walk with close vertical rail pales over the open lower level, under a roof near the main eave.
The numbered caption identifies the main entrance (1), sally-port (2), western gateway (3), NW and SE blockhouses (4,5), officers quarters (6), barracks (7), and magazine (8).
The roofed blockhouse lanterns as a retrospective representation, without a construction date.
what_it_does_not_supply: An eyewitness, independent testimony from 1803–1812, or a dated record of when the upper walks or blockhouse lanterns were built.
Any dimension, coordinate, bearing, measured roof slope, gallery depth, post section, rail height, baluster spacing or floor thickness.

Independent identification of every existing named range’s interior facade: the near faces are concealed, and the reconstruction’s main entrance and magazine arrangement must not displace Whistler’s contemporary measured plan.
Colour, material tone, or agreement between all pictorial reconstructions.
note: Use for visible form only. Whistler’s 1808 note directly attests two-storey barracks with galleries fronting the parade; this retrospective plate supports an inferred two-level interpretation, not an attested level count. Applying that treatment to all five first-fort ranges is stated in each gallery_storeys note. Metric details remain reconstructed. The book’s main-entrance building and magazine composition do not overrule the contemporary measured footprint register.
